Question 1: Bivariate Correlation

Scenario: The HR director wants to know if there is a relationship between an employee’s tenure and their stress levels.

1.1 Pearson Correlation Coefficient

pearson_result <- cor.test(clean_data$Years_Experience, clean_data$Stress_Index,
    method = "pearson")
pearson_result

1.4 Hypotheses and Interpretation

hypothesis_table <- data.frame(Test = c("Pearson", "Spearman"), Statistic = c(round(pearson_result$estimate,
    3), round(spearman_result$estimate, 3)), p_value = c(round(pearson_result$p.value,
    4), round(spearman_result$p.value, 4)), Conclusion = c(ifelse(pearson_result$p.value <
    0.05, "Reject H0", "Fail to reject H0"), ifelse(spearman_result$p.value < 0.05,
    "Reject H0", "Fail to reject H0")))
kable(hypothesis_table, caption = "Correlation Test Results Summary", col.names = c("Test",
    "Correlation Coefficient", "p-value", "Conclusion"))
Correlation Test Results Summary
Test Correlation Coefficient p-value Conclusion
cor Pearson -0.966 0 Reject H0
rho Spearman -0.974 0 Reject H0

Hypotheses:

  • Null Hypothesis (H₀): There is no relationship between years of experience and stress index (ρ = 0).
  • Alternative Hypothesis (H₁): There is a relationship between years of experience and stress index (ρ ≠ 0).

Interpretation:

Based on the scatterplot, the relationship between years of experience and stress index appears linear with a negative slope. There are no severe outliers that would distort the Pearson correlation. Therefore, the Pearson correlation is appropriate.

The Pearson correlation coefficient is r = -0.966, indicating a strong negative linear relationship. As years of experience increase, stress levels tend to decrease. With a p-value of 0, which is less than 0.05, we reject the null hypothesis. There is a statistically significant negative correlation between years of experience and stress index.

Interpretation:

The R-squared value is 0.8422, which means that 84.22% of the variance in productivity scores is explained by training hours. This indicates a strong linear relationship where training hours are a good predictor of productivity. The remaining 15.8% of the variance is due to other factors not included in the model.

3.2 Assumption Checks

3.2.1 Normality of Residuals

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

residuals <- residuals(model_multiple)
hist(residuals, main = "Histogram of Residuals", xlab = "Residuals", col = "lightblue",
    breaks = 15)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
shapiro_test <- shapiro.test(residuals)
cat("Shapiro-Wilk Normality Test:\n")
Shapiro-Wilk Normality Test:

W = 0.9747 
cat("p-value =", round(shapiro_test$p.value, 4), "\n")
p-value = 0.6745 
if (shapiro_test$p.value > 0.05) {
    cat("Conclusion: Residuals are normally distributed (fail to reject H0)\n")
} else {
    cat("Conclusion: Residuals deviate from normality (reject H0)\n")
}
Conclusion: Residuals are normally distributed (fail to reject H0)

Question 4: One-Way ANOVA

#Scenario:***The company wants to know if there is a significant difference in average productivity across the three departments.

4.1 Assumption Testing

4.1.1 Normality (Shapiro-Wilk by Group)

departments <- levels(clean_data$Department)
shapiro_results <- data.frame(Department = character(), W_statistic = numeric(),
    p_value = numeric(), Normal = character(), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
for (dept in departments) {
    subset_data <- clean_data$Productivity_Score[clean_data$Department == dept]
    test <- shapiro.test(subset_data)
    shapiro_results <- rbind(shapiro_results, data.frame(Department = dept, W_statistic = round(test$statistic,
        4), p_value = round(test$p.value, 4), Normal = ifelse(test$p.value > 0.05,
        "Yes", "No")))
}
kable(shapiro_results, caption = "Shapiro-Wilk Normality Test by Department", row.names = FALSE)
Shapiro-Wilk Normality Test by Department
Department W_statistic p_value Normal
HR 0.9658 0.8490 Yes
IT 0.9688 0.8796 Yes
Sales 0.9614 0.8017 Yes 
cat("\nNote: If p < 0.05, the data significantly deviates from normality.\n")

Note: If p < 0.05, the data significantly deviates from normality.

4.1.2 Homogeneity of Variances (Levene’s Test)

levene_test <- leveneTest(Productivity_Score ~ Department, data = clean_data)
kable(data.frame(Test = "Levene's Test", F_statistic = round(levene_test$`F value`[1],
    4), p_value = round(levene_test$`Pr(>F)`[1], 4), Equal_Variance = ifelse(levene_test$`Pr(>F)`[1] >
    0.05, "Yes", "No")), caption = "Levene's Test for Homogeneity of Variances")
Levene’s Test for Homogeneity of Variances
Test F_statistic p_value Equal_Variance
Levene’s Test 0.0259 0.9744 Yes 
cat("\nIf p > 0.05, we fail to reject the null hypothesis of equal variances.\n")

If p > 0.05, we fail to reject the null hypothesis of equal variances.

4.2 One-Way ANOVA

anova_model <- aov(Productivity_Score ~ Department, data = clean_data)
anova_summary <- summary(anova_model)
kable(anova_summary[[1]], caption = "One-Way ANOVA: Productivity ~ Department", digits = 4)

cat("\nANOVA p-value =", round(anova_p, 4), "\n")

ANOVA p-value = 0.4603 
if (anova_p < 0.05) {
    cat("Conclusion: There is a significant difference in productivity across departments.\n")
} else {
    cat("Conclusion: No significant difference in productivity across departments.\n")
}
Conclusion: No significant difference in productivity across departments.

4.3 Post-Hoc Test (Tukey’s HSD)

Question 5: Kruskal-Wallis H Test (Non-Parametric)

Scenario: The lead statistician notices that the productivity score for the Sales department is heavily skewed and violates the normality assumption.

5.1 Kruskal-Wallis Test

kruskal_result <- kruskal.test(Productivity_Score ~ Department, data = clean_data)
cat("Kruskal-Wallis Rank Sum Test:\n")
Kruskal-Wallis Rank Sum Test:
cat("Chi-squared =", round(kruskal_result$statistic, 4), "\n")
Chi-squared = 1.4013 
cat("df =", kruskal_result$parameter, "\n")
df = 2 
cat("p-value =", round(kruskal_result$p.value, 4), "\n")
p-value = 0.4963 
if (kruskal_result$p.value < 0.05) {
    cat("\nConclusion: There is a significant difference in productivity across departments.\n")
} else {
    cat("\nConclusion: No significant difference in productivity across departments.\n")
}

Conclusion: No significant difference in productivity across departments.

5.2 Comparison with ANOVA

comparison_table <- data.frame(Test = c("One-Way ANOVA", "Kruskal-Wallis H"), p_value = c(round(anova_p,
    4), round(kruskal_result$p.value, 4)), Conclusion = c(ifelse(anova_p < 0.05,
    "Significant difference", "No significant difference"), ifelse(kruskal_result$p.value <
    0.05, "Significant difference", "No significant difference")))
kable(comparison_table, caption = "Comparison of Parametric and Non-Parametric Tests",
    row.names = FALSE)
Comparison of Parametric and Non-Parametric Tests
Test p_value Conclusion
One-Way ANOVA 0.4603 No significant difference
Kruskal-Wallis H 0.4963 No significant difference

Interpretation:

  • One-Way ANOVA p-value: 0.4603
  • Kruskal-Wallis p-value: 0.4963

The conclusions are similar/different. The Kruskal-Wallis test is more robust to violations of normality and is appropriate when the Sales department’s productivity scores are heavily skewed. If both tests lead to the same conclusion, we can be more confident in our findings.

Question 6: Two-Way ANOVA

Scenario: Executive leadership wants to understand if productivity is influenced by Department, Work_Mode, and their interaction.

6.1 Two-Way ANOVA

twoway_model <- aov(Productivity_Score ~ Department * Work_Mode, data = clean_data)
twoway_summary <- summary(twoway_model)
kable(twoway_summary[[1]], caption = "Two-Way ANOVA: Productivity ~ Department * Work_Mode",
    digits = 4)
Two-Way ANOVA: Productivity ~ Department * Work_Mode
Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)
Department 2 416.6 208.3000 0.8465 0.4413
Work_Mode 1 907.5 907.5000 3.6880 0.0668
Department:Work_Mode 2 228.6 114.3000 0.4645 0.6340
Residuals 24 5905.6 246.0667 NA NA

6.2 Interaction Plot

interaction.plot(x.factor = clean_data$Work_Mode, trace.factor = clean_data$Department,
    response = clean_data$Productivity_Score, fun = mean, type = "b", col = c("red",
        "blue", "green"), pch = c(19, 17, 15), fixed = TRUE, legend = TRUE, xlab = "Work Mode",
    ylab = "Mean Productivity Score", trace.label = "Department", main = "Interaction Plot: Department × Work Mode")

clean_data %>%
    group_by(Department, Work_Mode) %>%
    summarise(Mean_Productivity = mean(Productivity_Score), .groups = "drop") %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = Work_Mode, y = Mean_Productivity, color = Department, group = Department)) +
    geom_line(size = 1.2) + geom_point(size = 4) + labs(title = "Interaction Plot: Department × Work Mode",
    subtitle = "Mean Productivity Score by Department and Work Mode", x = "Work Mode",
    y = "Mean Productivity Score", color = "Department") + theme_minimal() + theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

6.3 Post-Hoc Tests (if interaction is significant)

interaction_p <- twoway_summary[[1]]$`Pr(>F)`[3]
if (!is.na(interaction_p) && interaction_p < 0.05) {
    cat("Interaction effect is significant (p =", round(interaction_p, 4), ").\n")
    cat("Performing post-hoc analysis...\n\n")
    tukey_twoway <- TukeyHSD(twoway_model)
    kable(as.data.frame(tukey_twoway$`Department:Work_Mode`), caption = "Tukey's HSD for Department:Work_Mode Interaction",
        digits = 4)
} else {
    cat("Interaction effect is not significant (p =", round(interaction_p, 4), ").\n")
    cat("Interpreting main effects only.\n\n")
    tukey_dept <- TukeyHSD(aov(Productivity_Score ~ Department, data = clean_data))
    kable(as.data.frame(tukey_dept$Department), caption = "Tukey's HSD for Department Main Effect",
        digits = 4)
}

Automated Interpretation

Q1 — Correlation (Experience vs Stress). Pearson r = -0.966 (p = < 0.001); Spearman rho = -0.974 (p = < 0.001). There is a statistically significant relationship.

Q2 — Simple Regression (Training -> Productivity). The model explains 84.22% of the variance in Productivity (R2 = 0.8422, p = < 0.001).

Q3 — Multiple Regression (Experience + Training + Stress -> Productivity). Model R2 = 0.9666 (adj R2 = 0.9628, p = < 0.001). Statistically significant predictor(s) at alpha = 0.05: Training_Hours, Stress_Index.

Q4 — One-Way ANOVA (Productivity ~ Department). No significant difference in mean Productivity across departments. (p = 0.4603)

Q5 — Kruskal-Wallis H (Productivity ~ Department). The non-parametric test finds no significant difference between departments. (p = 0.4963) The conclusion is unchanged compared with the parametric ANOVA.

Q6 — Two-Way ANOVA (Productivity ~ Department * Work_Mode).

  • Department main effect: p = 0.4413 -> not significant.
  • Work_Mode main effect: p = 0.0668 -> not significant.
  • Department x Work_Mode interaction: p = 0.6340 -> no significant interaction; Work Mode effects are consistent across Departments.
